one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a Q&A explainer on Grace Poe's natural-born citizenship in 13 questions, expanding on two prior columns of June 14 and 21, 2015. Q1: Why is natural-born citizenship important? Only natural-born citizens are qualified to be president, VP, senator, congressman, or SC justice -- a contrary final decision would remove Poe as senator, bar her from running, and prohibit her from serving. Q2: What tribunals are authorized? The SET has jurisdiction over senator-qualification cases; the Comelec hears presidential-qualification petitions after COC filing; decisions may be elevated to the SC. Q3: Which Constitution governs? The 1935 Constitution, because it was the basic law in 1968 when Poe was born, listing five citizen sources: (1) those who were citizens at the adoption of the Constitution, (2) those born in the PH of foreign parents who before adoption had been elected to public office, (3) those whose fathers are citizens of the Philippines, (4) those whose mothers are citizens (with election upon majority), (5) those naturalized in accordance with law. The 1935 (and the current) Constitution also adopts 'the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the Nation' -- by this 'doctrine of incorporation,' customary international laws are as binding as statutes. Q4: Which international instruments? Mainly (a) the 1930 Hague Convention on the Conflict of Nationality Laws, (b) the 1948 UDHR, and (c) the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness -- nationality is synonymous with citizenship in international law. Q5: What 1961-Convention provision applies? Article 2: 'A foundling found in the territory of a Contracting State shall, in the absence of proof to the contrary, be considered to have been born in the territory of parents possessing the nationality of that State.' Q6: PH is not a signatory -- why bound? Because those provisions have become 'generally accepted principles of international law,' as binding as statutes passed by Congress. Q7: Who are natural-born citizens? Under the 1987 Constitution, 'those who are citizens of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect their Philippine citizenship.' Q8: Why is Poe natural-born? Because under Article 2 of the 1961 Convention, she -- a foundling found in Iloilo -- is deemed to have Filipino parents; perforce she is natural-born since her presumed father is accorded Philippine citizenship. Q9: Isn't she naturalized under item 5 -- naturalized in accordance with (international) law? No -- it was her parents who acquired Philippine citizenship pursuant to international law, but she derived her citizenship from her presumed Filipino father; thus she is a citizen from birth without having to do anything. Q10: May her biological father be proven to be an alien? Yes, but the burden of proof belongs to challengers; unless such proof is presented, her parents continue to be presumed Filipinos. Q11: She became a US citizen after marriage -- how did she reacquire natural-born status? By taking an oath of allegiance to the Philippines under the Dual Citizenship Law (RA 9225) and renouncing American citizenship pursuant to American law. Q12: Aside from the doctrine-of-incorporation interaction, can she prove natural-born status by other methods? Yes, by undergoing a DNA test showing her biological father is a Filipino; the SC has issued many decisions affirming the binding force of DNA tests. Q13: How are DNA tests conducted and can they conclusively prove parentage? Yes, if done according to the protocols laid down by the SC. More on this in a future column.
